title: Chair rent, brain fog, and holding it together
transcript:
[00:00:08] INT: Right, the recorder is going now. Thanks so much for agreeing to speak with me today for the Northshire University study on Working with Long COVID. Just to start off, could you tell me a little bit about yourself and your household?
[00:00:24] P: Yeah, of course. Um, so I'm Tracey Henderson, I'm 45, and I live in Ketteridge—just up in the Millfield area, 42 Larkspur Close. It's me and my two kids. Callum's fourteen now, going on thirty, you know how they are, and Maisie's nine. I'm a single parent of two, been on my own since my ex-husband Gary moved out about five years ago. So, yeah, it's a busy house, or it used to be before all this started.
[00:01:02] INT: And what were you doing for work before you got ill?
[00:01:07] P: I'm a self-employed hairdresser. Been doing it since I left college. I rent a chair at a little salon called Scissors & Sheen down on the High Street. The owner's Brenda Kowalski—lovely woman, known her years. Before COVID, I was doing forty, forty-five hours a week easily. I'd built up a really solid client base, and my little niche was 1940s vintage bridal styling—victory rolls, pin curls, all that retro stuff. Weddings on Saturdays, regular cuts and colours Tuesday to Friday. I was clearing about £480 a week after paying Brenda her £180 a week chair rent. It wasn't a fortune, don't get me wrong, but it kept us going, paid the bills, let me take the kids to the coast in the summer.
[00:02:08] INT: It sounds like you really loved it.
[00:02:11] P: Oh, I adored it. Honestly, I'm a chatterbox, I love being on my feet, having a laugh with the regulars. And outside of work, I was always on the go. I used to do competitive bell-ringing up at St. Mary's—yeah, I know, bit of an odd one! People always laugh when I tell them, but it's proper physical work, pulling those ropes, and it was my one night a week just for me. Haven't been up that tower in over two years now. Makes me want to cry just thinking about it.
[00:02:51] INT: I'm sorry, Tracey. Take your time. When did you first catch COVID?
[00:02:58] P: It was the 14th of November 2021. I remember the exact date because it was the day after Maisie's school fair. I came down with it hard—high fever, awful cough, couldn't lift my head off the pillow for ten days. Gary actually had to take the kids for a week, which is a miracle in itself. Anyway, the cough cleared up, I tested negative, and I thought, right, back to normal. Except it wasn't. I went back to the salon in December and after two hours I felt like someone had unplugged me from the wall. Just this bone-deep, crushing fatigue. Like wading through wet concrete.
[00:03:54] INT: How did that show up in the actual day-to-day work at Scissors & Sheen?
[00:04:01] P: Oh, God, it was terrifying at first. It wasn't just the tiredness, it was the brain fog. I've been mixing colour for twenty-five years, I could do it in my sleep. One Tuesday, Mrs. Paton came in—she's been coming to me for a decade, always has the exact same ash blonde tint. I stood in the back room staring at the tubes and I completely blanked. Didn't know the ratio, didn't know which developer to use. I actually had to ask Jade, the junior stylist who's nineteen, to check my bowl for me. I went into the toilet and just sobbed. And then the standing—standing at the chair for hours started giving me these awful dizzy spells. My heart would just hammer out of nowhere, like I'd sprinted up a hill, just from blow-drying someone's fringe.
[00:05:08] INT: That must have been so frightening, especially when you're self-employed and your income depends on being there.
[00:05:15] P: Exactly. You don't work, you don't get paid. There's no sick pay when you're renting a chair. For months I just pushed through, and then I'd come home and crash on the sofa, couldn't even cook tea for Callum and Maisie. Callum ended up making beans on toast for his sister half the week. That's when the guilt really kicks in, isn't it? You feel like you're failing as a mum and failing at your job.
[00:05:50] INT: When did you decide to tell Brenda what was going on?
[00:05:56] P: It was March 2022. I'd had a really bad turn right in the middle of a perm—had to sit down on the floor by the basins because the room was spinning. Brenda came over and said, "Tracey, you're grey, what is going on with you?" So I just broke down and told her everything. That the doctors were saying it looked like Long COVID, that I couldn't cope with the full days anymore. I was petrified she'd say she needed someone in that chair who could pay full rent.
[00:06:35] INT: How did she react?
[00:06:38] P: To be fair to Brenda, she was brilliant at first. She gave me a massive hug and said we'd figure it out. She let me bring in a saddle stool so I could sit while cutting, and she said I could block out twenty-minute gaps between clients so I could sit in the staffroom with my feet up. She even dropped my chair rent to a daily rate when I cut down to three days a week. It was a lifeline, honestly. Though, um, it's got harder over time. In September 2023 I had a massive relapse after doing a wedding—stupidly thought I could manage a bridal party of four—and I had to drop down to just two half-days. Brenda's still kind, but I can tell she's stretched. She's got overheads, electricity's gone through the roof, and my chair's sitting empty half the week. I constantly feel like I'm on borrowed time.
[00:07:48] INT: Let's talk a bit about the financial side of dropping to two half-days. How have you managed?
[00:07:56] P: Barely. That's the honest truth. I'm taking home maybe £165 a week now on a good week, and some weeks if I have a flare-up and have to cancel clients, it's nothing. I had to swallow my pride and apply for Universal Credit. That gives me a top-up of about £290 a month, depending on what I earn. And then a friend told me to apply for PIP. Oh, blimey, what a nightmare that was. The forms are like a novel, and when you've got brain fog, trying to explain how you can't wash your own hair without resting for an hour is just exhausting.
[00:08:45] INT: Did you have to go through an assessment for PIP?
[00:08:49] P: Yeah, had a phone assessment on the 12th of May. I was a nervous wreck. I've actually still got the DWP letter right here on the kitchen table—hang on, let me look at it—yeah, reference PIP-88412-TH. They turned me down at first, gave me zero points! Said because I still worked a few hours as a hairdresser, I must be fine. I had to do a mandatory reconsideration with a letter from my clinic, and eventually they awarded me the standard daily living rate, which is £72.65 a week. It helps, don't get me wrong, it pays for the food shop, mostly. But I've had to cancel the kids' swimming lessons, I'm constantly juggling the gas bill. Gary pays the bare minimum child maintenance and not a penny more. He still thinks I'm just "a bit run down."
[00:09:56] INT: That's so tough, not being believed by people close to you. What has your experience been like with healthcare?
[00:10:05] P: Mixed, to put it politely. I'm at Bramley Brook Medical Practice. The first GP I saw, Dr. Patel, basically patted my hand and told me I was a stressed single mum going through perimenopause. Offered me antidepressants and sent me on my way. I felt like I was going mad. Luckily, a couple of months later I saw Dr. O'Connor at the same surgery, and she actually listened. She did a standing heart rate test right there in the room—my pulse shot up by forty beats a minute just standing up. She referred me to the Long COVID clinic over at St. Jude's General Hospital.
[00:10:55] INT: How long did you have to wait for St. Jude's?
[00:10:59] P: About eight months. I was ringing them every fortnight, rattling off my NHS number—999 482 1037—just begging for a cancellation. When I finally got in, it was such a relief just to be told, "No, you're not making this up." They diagnosed me with Long COVID and Postural Tachycardia Syndrome—PoTS—and explained about post-exertional malaise. That was a lightbulb moment, realising that pushing through on a Tuesday was why I couldn't get out of bed on a Thursday.
[00:11:41] INT: Have they been able to offer you any treatments or medications?
[00:11:46] P: They put me on propranolol for the racing heart, which definitely takes the edge off the dizzy spells, though it makes my hands freezing cold. I'm also on fexofenadine—just an antihistamine, apparently it helps some people with the inflammation—and high-dose vitamin D. And they gave me pacing worksheets. Which are great in theory, you know, "stop before you're tired," but try telling a nine-year-old who needs her PE kit washed that Mummy's out of spoons.
[00:12:26] INT: You mentioned earlier feeling like you're failing as a mum. How has all of this affected your sense of who you are?
[00:12:35] P: Oh, completely shattered it. I don't recognise myself anymore. I used to be the one everyone came to—at the salon, in the family, at church. I was capable, I was loud, I had my hair done, my makeup on. Now I spend half my life in joggers on the sofa. Last summer I missed Maisie's sports day because I'd overdone it at work the day before and literally couldn't walk to the school gates. She was so sweet about it, said "Don't worry Mummy, I'll run extra fast for you," and it just broke my heart. And Callum's had to grow up way too fast. He shouldn't be asking me if I've taken my tablets.
[00:13:28] INT: Do you feel like you're grieving the old Tracey?
[00:13:33] P: Yeah. That's the exact word for it. Grief. I've still got all my vintage styling pins and my good Japanese scissors in my kit bag, and sometimes I look at them and wonder if I'll ever do a full Saturday wedding again. Probably not. I'm trying to accept that maybe this is just my life now, smaller and slower, but it's hard when you're 45 and you feel like you're eighty-five.
[00:14:09] INT: Tracey, thank you so much for being so open with me today. I know it takes a lot of energy to talk through all of this, so I don't want to keep you much longer. Just before we finish, is there anything else you'd like to add about working with Long COVID?
[00:14:27] P: Just that self-employed people fall completely through the cracks. Everyone talks about HR departments and phased returns and occupational health, and I'm like, I am my own HR department! If I don't stand behind that chair, the money stops. There needs to be a proper safety net for people like me.
[00:14:53] INT: That's a really important point, thank you. Right, I'll stop the recording in a second, and I just need to double-check where to send your thank-you voucher and the study summary when it's ready.
[00:15:06] P: Oh, lovely. My email's tracey.henderson81@example.com, and if you need to text me anything, my mobile is 07700 900412. Thanks for listening, honestly, it's nice to feel heard for once.
